teaching.causalExplanation: Health is what's called a contested idea. That means sensible people disagree about where its edges are. The definition you'll meet most often comes from the World Health Organization. It says health is "a state of complete physical, mental and social wellbeing and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity." It's been part of the organisation's constitution since that came into force in 1948, and the wording hasn't changed since. Two phrases do most of the work. "Not merely the absence of disease" makes health something you have, not just a gap where illness isn't. Older medical ideas worked the other way round, so anyone without a diagnosis counted as healthy by default. And "physical, mental and social" brings three dimensions inside health. So someone with no disease, but no sleep, no friends and nowhere secure to live, isn't healthy on this definition. That's why governments quote it. It lets them treat housing and loneliness as health problems. Now underline the word "complete". It's where the main criticism lands. If health means complete wellbeing in all three dimensions, then on a strict reading almost nobody is healthy at any given moment. And it's harsh on people living with a chronic condition or a disability, like our athlete with asthma, who'd count as unhealthy for life. But that doesn't make the definition useless. It was written as an aim for health systems, a statement of what they should work towards, not a test for sorting people into healthy and unhealthy.

If health means complete wellbeing in all three dimensions, then on a strict reading almost nobody is healthy at any given moment. It was written as an aim for health systems, a statement of what they should work towards, not a test for sorting people into healthy and unhealthy.

And it's harsh on people living with a chronic condition or a disability, like our athlete with asthma, who'd count as unhealthy for life. But that doesn't make the definition useless. It was written as an aim for health systems, a statement of what they should work towards, not a test for sorting people into healthy and unhealthy.

scenes.teachingReason: The WHO definition isn't the only meaning in use, and the others aren't just worse versions of it. Two are narrower. The biomedical meaning says health is the absence of diagnosable disease or injury. It's precise and testable, which is exactly what a doctor needs at three in the morning, but it says almost nothing about whether a life is going well. Under it, our athlete isn't healthy. The functional meaning says health is being able to do what your life asks of you. Under that one, they clearly are.

scenes.teachingReason: One meaning is wider than the WHO's. The holistic meaning sees the whole person in their whole context, not a body on its own. In Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health, this idea is called social and emotional wellbeing. It covers connection to body, to mind and emotions, to family and kinship, community, culture, Country, and spirituality and ancestors. And it treats a person's health and their community's health as one thing, not two separate topics.

scenes.teachingReason: So why do people choose different meanings? It isn't random. People tend to define health by what health has cost or given them. A sixteen-year-old often means energy and fitness, while an eighty-year-old means getting to the shops on their own. Living with a condition moves people from "nothing wrong" to "managing it well". Culture sets whether health belongs to one body or to a family and community. A labourer needs a different body from an accountant. And people with fewer resources often set the bar where they can actually reach it. None of these is wrong. Each meaning is situated: built by someone, somewhere, for a purpose.

scenes.teachingReason: When a question says compare, don't describe one meaning and then the other, and don't just pick a winner. Put them side by side on the same three questions. What does each one count? What does it leave out? And whose work does it make possible? Try it on our athlete. Biomedical counts the diagnosis, so it calls them unwell. Functional counts what they can do, so it calls them healthy. Biomedical leaves out how their life is going, while functional has no fixed line. One serves the doctor, the other serves the person. Neither is wrong. They're built for different jobs.

On "Next" the chips and thumbnail leave and the meanings ladder returns at the left of centre (about 70 per cent of frame height) with the WHO rung lit blue and the others in full-ink grey; on "the three dimensions" the words "physical", "mental" and "social" on the WHO rung glow amber; a "Next" chip slides in at the lower right: "Next: what makes health change?" **This is the handoff frame; v02 opens from it.** Hold half a second before the notes.
motionTools: Cue-directed changes described in the design

scenes.motionPurpose:
Heading on screen: "Key notes: what to write in your book".

1. WHO: complete physical, mental and social wellbeing, not merely no disease.
2. Criticism: "complete" excludes almost everyone. Defence: an aim, not a test.
3. Narrow to wide: biomedical, functional, WHO, holistic.
4. Meanings are situated by age, illness, culture, work and circumstance.
5. Compare: what each counts, leaves out, and is useful for.

Memory card (framed in dark ink, beside the notes; the scene 10 card): "Widen: more relevant, less precise" and "Compare: counts / leaves out / useful for". Notes 38 px in the role colours (note 3 in its four rung colours, the others ink); each bullet one line of at most 86 characters. Hold about 45 seconds in all.
